items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: I learned more from him about music, and what music can do for people

ctx.x: Now you're talking about New Orleans.

Yeah, that's right. I always tell people like Bunk Johnson, I studied with some other very great musicians, I will say Arnold Schoenberg, whom some people consider as at least one of the two or three greatest modern composers, and other, not to knock any of the classical musicians, but as I always say, Bunk had more music in him, and I learned more from him about music, and what music can do for people, and what its real place is in life, and I ever did before.
You mean he expressed this in his own personality as well as in his music?

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: I asked him about Bunk 2 where I could find Bunk Johnson and we didn't know his name for sure... I remember on the way out, then I was collecting money for Bunk's teeth at that time, too. Ramsey and I were trying to get money together to have Dr. Bessie get a set of false teeth for Bunk.

ctx.x: but it was really funny I couldn't act like I didn't appreciate it

I thanked her and all I don't know what happened to the catalog but that's when I asked him about Bunk 2 where I could find Bunk Johnson and we didn't know his name for sure and he did illustrated you might say demonstrated Bunk's style just by singing

and was it Jasmine that started an interest again in New Orleans music or was it the so called Dixieland revival as it's popularly called with the issuing of some of the mostly records of people like Bunk Johnson

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: In the old days, they had these routines Bunkies talked about and Baby Dodds used to talk about it too.

ctx.x: They don't play the lead? No, they just want to sit there and rest. Oh, I see. And Jim said, that's no way to do.

I came across the old notes I'd taken once over at Preservation Hall about five or six years ago, or maybe ten years ago, I think they were. I happened to be sitting out in the carriageway there on those benches, and Jim was there. He wasn't playing that night. And so I copied down the remarks he was making after he left. I didn't copy them down, but mostly word for word. And he would say, what kind of a band, what kind of a trumpet player? Where's the trumpet player? He'd keep saying, where's the trumpet player?…
I think it was King Oliver who said that he wanted his band to be able to play so soft they could hear the dancers shuffling.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: Bunk, if he was a friend, he'd do anything for you. ... I mean, Bunk was a wonderful guy.

ctx.x: Yeah. But they'd gone together... Anyway, say, 10 years or so ago, quite a while back. Anyway, George Barquet's brother, Sheil, who wasn't as well-known as George, down here at least, had passed for white for years. I know Mineta says he met him once on Canal Street after he started passing, and he said, well, I like it better. I forget. I have that in some of the Mineta interviews. Some of that stuff I'll copy, too, later on, which is on tape. He likes it better. Mineta sort of, you know, he wasn't mad at him or…
